items.title: Multi-tenant support for divergent tenant schemas

labels.name: .Team/UXWest
labels.description: UX West - use for bugs and feature requests

items.body:
**What problem will this feature request solve?**

The current multi-tenant tooling assumes one of following data shapes:
* Per-tenant databases with identical schemas with db routing
* A single multi-tenant database with row-level security / sandboxing
* A singel multi-tenant database with impersonation

Each shape assumes identical tenant schemas, while some customers might see their tenant schemas diverge: a shared "generic" schema plus small per-tenant or per-version customizations (a few tenant specific tables, columns or an extra schema with customer controlled data).

These customers are forced into an all-manual workflow: hand-managing groups, collections, permissions, and serialization across their tenants and databases.


**Describe the solution you'd like.**

Extend the tenant tooling, db routing, db permissions  so a common schema can be shared across tenants while allowing controlled per-tenant divergence, without hand-templatizing everything through serialization. 

Two complementary directions (either would materially help; ideally both):

*Option A — Hybrid database routing (shared schema + per-tenant additions).*
Keep the shared "generic" schema managed once on the primary/template database and fanned out to all tenants as today, but let each destination database **catalog and expose its own tenant-specific tables / sub-schemas** on top of the shared template. In short: routing that tolerates a superset schema per tenant instead of requiring byte-for-byte identical schemas.

*Option B — Per-tenant database tagging (scoped connections).*
Allow a database connection to be **tagged to one or more specific tenants**. A tagged database is queryable only by the listed tenants and is invisible to all others. This gives a clean, declarative way to attach a tenant's divergent/custom data as its own connection while the shared datasets stay common — instead of encoding the isolation manually via groups, collections, and permission grants. It extends primitives the [tenants model](https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/embedding/tenants#data-permissions-for-tenants) already exposes: the system-defined `@tenant.slug` attribute is the natural tag key, and the existing **All tenant users** / per-tenant groups are the natural scope — so a tagged database simply grants data access to the listed tenant(s) and is hidden from the rest.


**How does this feature request impact you?**

Request from a Pro / Enterprise trialer


**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Options explored with the customer before filing this (all workable but insufficient at scale):

- **Database routing (identical-schema model)** — doesn't fit: routing syncs only the primary DB and assumes identical schemas, so per-tenant custom tables are dropped.
Customers would need to resort to using native questions or models to query their custom schemas, and some native features such as linked filters, drop-down values would not work. 

- **Tenants feature** — built as convenience sugar over the permission system for the two shapes above. 
Tenant data permissions are assigned via the **All tenant users** group plus the per-tenant groups and cross-tenant segregation is enforced via db routing (separate DBs) *or* a shared DB with Row/Column Security or Impersonation. 
None of these paths can represent a per-tenant schema that diverges from a shared template.

- **Manual groups + collections + per-tenant permissions, templatized via serialization blueprints and the API (the pragmatic path chosen)** — functional, but all-manual: it fans out configuration across hundreds of databases, multiplies the metadata sync surface (tables × columns × tenants), and offers no migration path to a first-class feature later. 
It also surfaces adjacent scale pain — per-tenant database connections.


**Additional context about the requestor**

- Deployment: Metabase Cloud, BigQuery data warehouse, tenant data is located in separate BQ projects or datasets. The theme of the request applies to any dwh type equally.
- Topology per tenant: one shared "generic" schema (identical across all tenants) + one "custom" schema (per-tenant divergence).
- Adjacent concerns the customer raised that this feature would relieve: scalability of hundreds of database connections, and the flat/non-searchable admin Databases UI at that scale.
- The customer explicitly asked whether to **wait for a proper feature or continue the manual serialization approach** . Once implemented, a migration path from the manual/serialization world into a first-class model would be valuable.

items.title: [security] Any authenticated user can flush and rebuild every datasource connection and the Mondrian schema cache via GET /discover/refresh (no role check, {username} ignored)

labels.name: security
labels.description: Created by Hive for agent-filed issue provenance

items.body:
**Saiku version:** `development` @ `39c00634f` (origin/development, 2026-11-10)
**How are you running Saiku?** Built from source — applies to the launcher JAR, the Docker image (`ghcr.io/spiculedata/saiku`) and WAR deployments; see *Impact* for per-mode notes.
**Environment:** any JDK 21+/22; any browser; database behind the datasource.

## Severity

**LOW** — any authenticated user (ROLE_USER) can call `GET /rest/saiku/{username}/discover/refresh` to reload **all** datasources and `GET /rest/saiku/{username}/discover/{connection}/refresh` to reload a named one. The refresh evicts the cached connection, calls `clearCache()` which `flushSchemaCache()` on the Mondrian `RolapConnection`, and rebuilds. The `{username}` path segment is **not** compared to the caller's principal, so any user can trigger a global cache flush. This is an availability / resource-abuse vector: a flush discards Mondrian's warmed schema and segment caches for every tenant, so all subsequent queries pay a cold-cache rebuild (seconds to tens of seconds on large cubes / cold warehouses), and a user can hold the server in a permanently cold state by looping the call. The endpoint is *intentionally* un-gated (saiku#1903) so the SPA's cube picker can poll it; this finding is that "re-load descriptors" was treated as harmless while the side effect is a full cache flush of shared state. LOW because it does not disclose or corrupt data and needs an authenticated account, but it is a cheap denial-of-service lever available to the lowest-privileged user. CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling), CWE-284 (Improper Access Control).

## Affected files

- `saiku-core/saiku-web/src/main/java/org/saiku/web/rest/resources/OlapDiscoverResource.java:42` — class `@Path("/saiku/{username}/discover")`; `{username}` is never read or compared to the principal
- `saiku-core/saiku-web/src/main/java/org/saiku/web/rest/resources/OlapDiscoverResource.java:144-167` — `GET /refresh` → `refreshAllConnections()` + `getAllConnections()`; javadoc "Deliberately NOT admin-gated (saiku#1903)"
- `saiku-core/saiku-web/src/main/java/org/saiku/web/rest/resources/OlapDiscoverResource.java:169-186` — `GET /{connection}/refresh` → `refreshConnection(name)`
- `saiku-core/saiku-service/src/main/java/org/saiku/service/olap/OlapDiscoverService.java:83-98` — `refreshAllConnections()` / `refreshConnection(name)` delegate to the connection manager
- `saiku-core/saiku-service/src/main/java/org/saiku/datasources/connection/AbstractConnectionManager.java:144-178` — `refreshAllConnections()` loops datasources and `refreshConnection()` each; `refreshConnection()` also `CubeMetadataVersions.bump(name)`
- `saiku-core/saiku-web/src/main/java/org/saiku/web/core/SecurityAwareConnectionManager.java:167-181` — `refreshInternalConnection()`: `connections.remove(newName)` + `con.clearCache()` + rebuild
- `saiku-core/saiku-service/src/main/java/org/saiku/datasources/connection/SaikuOlapConnection.java:232-238` — `clearCache()` → `rcon.getCacheControl(null).flushSchemaCache()` (process-wide Mondrian schema cache)
- `saiku-webapp/src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/applicationContext-saiku.xml:363` — this route falls under `/rest/**` → `isFullyAuthenticated()` (no role gate)

## Description

`OlapDiscoverResource` is mounted at `/saiku/{username}/discover`. The `{username}` segment is decorative — it appears in the class `@Path` but no method reads it, and nothing compares it to `SecurityContextHolder`'s principal. So a user may call the refresh endpoints with any `{username}` (their own, another user's, anything), and the only access control is the generic `/rest/** → isFullyAuthenticated()` rule.

`GET /refresh` calls `olapDiscoverService.refreshAllConnections()`, which iterates the current user's visible datasources and calls `refreshConnection(name)` on each. `refreshConnection` → `SecurityAwareConnectionManager.refreshInternalConnection`, which removes the cached `ISaikuConnection` and calls `con.clearCache()` before rebuilding. For an OLAP connection `clearCache()` unwraps the `RolapConnection` and calls `getCacheControl(null).flushSchemaCache()` — this flushes Mondrian's **schema cache**, which is process-global shared state, not per-user. `refreshConnection` additionally calls `CubeMetadataVersions.bump(name)`, invalidating the cellset cache for that connection. `GET /{connection}/refresh` does the same for one named connection.

saiku#1903 deliberately left these un-gated so the workbench cube picker can poll `/discover/refresh` to pick up late-arriving cubes (the saiku-cloud warming model — `saiku-ui/src/lib/stores/datasources.svelte.ts:73` polls every 3s). The stated justification (`OlapDiscoverResource.java:146-151`) is that a refresh "can only re-load descriptors an administrator was able to write" and every descriptor is validated by `JdbcUrlPolicy`. That reasoning covers *what gets loaded*; it does not cover the *side effect* — flushing the shared Mondrian schema/segment cache and the cellset cache on demand, which is an availability cost borne by all users, and `{username}` offers no scoping at all. A user can loop `GET /rest/saiku/anything/discover/refresh` and keep every cube's cache cold.

## Code walkthrough (entry point → sink)

1. `saiku-core/saiku-web/src/main/java/org/saiku/web/rest/resources/OlapDiscoverResource.java:42` — the `{username}` is in the path but unused for authorization:
   ```java
   @Path("/saiku/{username}/discover")
   public class OlapDiscoverResource implements Serializable {
   ```
2. `OlapDiscoverResource.java:155-167` — `GET /refresh`, no role check, no principal comparison:
   ```java
   @GET
   @Produces({"application/json"})
   @Path("/refresh")
   public List<SaikuConnection> refreshConnections() {
       try {
           olapDiscoverService.refreshAllConnections();
           return olapDiscoverService.getAllConnections();
       } catch (Exception e) {
           ...
   ```
3. `saiku-core/saiku-service/src/main/java/org/saiku/datasources/connection/AbstractConnectionManager.java:144-167` — refresh loops all visible datasources and bumps the cellset-cache epoch per connection:
   ```java
   public void refreshAllConnections() {
       ds.load();
       ...
       for (String name : ds.getDatasources(roles).keySet()) {
           try {
               refreshConnection(name);
   ...
   public void refreshConnection(String name) {
       ...
       ISaikuConnection con = refreshInternalConnection(name, datasource);
       ...
       org.saiku.service.cache.CubeMetadataVersions.bump(name);
   }
   ```
4. `saiku-core/saiku-web/src/main/java/org/saiku/web/core/SecurityAwareConnectionManager.java:167-180` — evicts the cached connection and clears its cache:
   ```java
   protected ISaikuConnection refreshInternalConnection(String name, SaikuDatasource datasource) {
       try {
           String newName = resolveConnectionKey(name, datasource);
           ISaikuConnection con = connections.remove(newName);
           if (con != null) {
               con.clearCache();
           }
           return getInternalConnection(name, datasource);
   ```
5. `saiku-core/saiku-service/src/main/java/org/saiku/datasources/connection/SaikuOlapConnection.java:232-238` — the shared Mondrian schema cache is flushed:
   ```java
   public boolean clearCache() throws Exception {
       if (olapConnection.isWrapperFor(RolapConnection.class)) {
           log.info("Clearing cache");
           RolapConnection rcon = olapConnection.unwrap(RolapConnection.class);
           rcon.getCacheControl(null).flushSchemaCache();
       }
       return true;
   }
   ```

## Steps to reproduce

**Preconditions:** launcher JAR with the FoodMart datasource warmed (run a query so Mondrian's schema/segment caches are populated). Any authenticated user. GET needs no CSRF token.

1. As any user, flush everything:
   ```bash
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u 'viewer:admin' \
     'http://localhost:8080/rest/saiku/not-my-username/discover/refresh'
   ```
   Returns `200` — note `{username}` is a value that is not the caller and is accepted. The server log shows "Clearing cache" per connection.
2. Immediately re-run a previously fast query; observe the first post-flush execution is markedly slower (cold Mondrian schema/segment cache rebuild), and any in-flight query on that connection is affected by the eviction.
3. Loop the call (`while true; do curl ... /discover/refresh; done`) and observe every cube stays cold — queries never benefit from Mondrian caching while the loop runs.
4. Single connection variant:
   ```bash
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u 'viewer:admin' \
     'http://localhost:8080/rest/saiku/x/discover/foodmart/refresh'
   ```

## Expected behaviour

A full/per-connection cache flush is restricted (ROLE_ADMIN), or at minimum scoped to the caller's own connection set and rate-limited, so a low-privileged user cannot repeatedly flush shared Mondrian/cellset caches and hold the server cold. The SPA's benign "pick up new cubes" poll is served without a destructive schema flush, or by a separate, cheap, non-flushing discovery call.

## Actual behaviour

Any authenticated user, with any `{username}`, can flush and rebuild all (or a named) datasource connections and the shared Mondrian schema cache, unthrottled.

## Impact

Who: every deployment; the attacker is any authenticated user (ROLE_USER), the victims are all other users and tenants sharing the JVM. What: on each call, every visible datasource's cached connection is evicted and rebuilt, Mondrian's shared schema cache is flushed (`flushSchemaCache()`), and the cellset cache epoch is bumped — so all warm state is lost. In-flight queries on evicted connections are affected, the next query per cube pays a full cold schema load and segment re-fetch (seconds to tens of seconds on large cubes or cold cloud warehouses), and a tight loop keeps the server permanently cold (effective denial of service plus warehouse cost from repeated re-scans). No data disclosure or modification; the datasource descriptors loaded are still the admin-written, `JdbcUrlPolicy`-validated ones.

- **Launcher JAR** (`java -jar saiku-<version>.jar serve`): affected; a single user loop degrades the whole instance.
- **Docker image**: affected identically.
- **WAR in own servlet container**: affected identically.
- **Embedded in saiku-cloud**: affected and most serious — one tenant's low-privileged user can flush the shared Mondrian schema cache and rebuild connections for every tenant on the node, and repeated cold loads against pay-per-query warehouses (Snowflake/BigQuery) convert the availability hit into direct cost for other tenants.

## Suggested fix

1. **Separate "discover new cubes" from "flush caches."** The SPA poll needs the former; make `refreshConnections()`/`refreshConnection()` perform a *non-destructive* reconcile (reload descriptors, add newly-appeared connections) without calling `clearCache()`/`flushSchemaCache()` on existing warm connections. Give the destructive flush its own endpoint.
2. **Gate the destructive flush with ROLE_ADMIN.** The new flush endpoint carries `@RolesAllowed("ROLE_ADMIN")` and a matching URL gate (move it under `/rest/saiku/admin/**`, which already has `hasRole('ADMIN')`), mirroring `AdminResource`.
3. **If the poll must stay open, scope and throttle it.** Compare `{username}` to the principal (or drop it from the path), restrict `refreshAllConnections` to the caller's own visible connection set, and add a short per-principal rate limit (the codebase already has rate limiters, e.g. `aiOssieAskRateLimiter`) so a loop cannot keep caches cold.
4. Update the `OlapDiscoverResource.java:146-151` javadoc to reflect that the open endpoint no longer flushes shared caches (or is admin-gated).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A ROLE_USER-only caller cannot trigger a Mondrian `flushSchemaCache()` / full connection rebuild; the destructive flush returns 403 for non-admins.
- [ ] The SPA cube-picker poll still discovers newly-added cubes without flushing warm caches.
- [ ] `{username}` is either compared to the principal or removed from the authorization-relevant path; a non-matching `{username}` cannot widen access.
- [ ] A rapid loop of the remaining open discovery endpoint does not keep caches cold (non-destructive and/or rate-limited).
- [ ] regression test(s) listed under *Acceptance tests* are added and green

## Acceptance tests

- `OlapDiscoverResourceRefreshAuthTest.flush_nonAdmin_returns403` (unit, saiku-web): with a ROLE_USER `SecurityContext`, call the (new) flush endpoint; assert 403 and that `olapDiscoverService.refreshAllConnections()` was not invoked. Fails today (200, flush runs).
- `OlapDiscoverResourceRefreshAuthTest.discover_nonAdmin_reconcilesWithoutClearingCache` (unit): call the open discovery endpoint; assert connection `clearCache()` is not invoked on already-warm connections.
- `AbstractConnectionManagerTest.reconcile_doesNotFlushSchemaCache` (unit, saiku-service): assert the non-destructive reconcile path never calls `clearCache()`/`flushSchemaCache()`.
- `UrlGateHardeningIT.discoverFlush_nonAdmin_403` (launcher integration, extend `UrlGateHardeningIT`): `harness.getAuth("viewer","admin","/rest/saiku/x/discover/refresh")` (or the new flush path) → 403 for the destructive variant; the benign discovery variant → 200. Fails today.
- `OlapDiscoverIT.refreshLoop_doesNotKeepCubesCold` (launcher integration): warm a query, loop the open discovery endpoint, assert query latency stays warm (no repeated schema flush).

## Related

- #1903 — "any authenticated user could register/load a datasource → RCE" (closed); that fix left `/discover/refresh` deliberately open, which is the decision this finding revisits for the cache-flush side effect
- #2326 — `/discover/refresh` rebuilds Mondrian connections but does not invalidate the AI schema cache, so it cannot be used to recover from the H4 poisoning either; the refresh/invalidation story should be unified

## Found by

Internal security review, 2026-11-10.

items.title: security: default catalogs let every stardelt-users member read/write other users' tables

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Next: the milestone cannot ship without it

milestone.title: v0.7
milestone.description: AI and ML: assistant and tools, AI functions, vector search, feature store, tracking, serving, GPU

items.body:
## What happened

Two unrelated use-case users can read and modify each other's tables in the default catalogs:

- `mobility.analyst` (group `mobility-analytics`) uploaded
  `warehouse.qa_cross.secret_by_mobility`.
- `retail.analyst` (group `retail-analytics`, not in mobility-analytics) queried it successfully:
  `SELECT * FROM warehouse.qa_cross.secret_by_mobility` → the row
  `only mobility should see this?`.
- `retail.analyst` could also create `warehouse.qa_cross.planted_by_retail`; the mobility user
  could see/drop it. Cleaned up after the test.

The use-case catalogs are isolated correctly (`retail` vs `mobility` both deny cross-access), but
the baseline catalogs are not.

## Cause

The dev seed grants `browse`, `select`, `write` and `create` to `stardelt-users` on
`warehouse`, `bronze`, `silver`, `gold` and `shared` (`dev/seed/catalogs.yaml`). Every platform
user is in `stardelt-users`, so the default catalogs are effectively a shared read/write area.
`shared` may be intentional; `warehouse`/`bronze`/`silver`/`gold` are the platform's default data
plane and are not tenant-safe.

## Impact

- A user can read another team's data if either team uses `warehouse`/`bronze`/`silver`/`gold`.
- A user can overwrite/drop another team's tables in those catalogs (`CREATE OR REPLACE`, `DROP`,
  `ROLLBACK_TO_SNAPSHOT` where permitted).
- The UI and docs present “Load data” as writing to `warehouse` (nova#443), so a user following the
  default path puts data into the shared area without a warning.
- The use-case catalogs demonstrate that isolation works; the default layout undermines it.

## Expected / options

- Make the baseline catalogs read-only to `stardelt-users` (select/browse) and move writes to
  group-owned use-case catalogs; or
- Keep `shared` as the one explicit shared write area, and make `warehouse`/`bronze`/`silver`/`gold`
  owner-group/administrator-only; or
- At minimum, mark the default catalogs as shared in the UI and warn on write/upload; the seed
  should state that they are not tenant-isolated.

## Acceptance

1. A second use-case user cannot read or write a table created by the first in
   `warehouse`/`bronze`/`silver`/`gold`.
2. `shared` remains the documented shared area (if that is the chosen design).
3. Upload/transfer target the catalog the user chose (see nova#443).
4. A test covers cross-user read/write denial in the baseline catalogs.

## Evidence

- `cross-upload.json` / `cross-read.json` in `.qa-mobility/features/`.
- Live test 2026-11-02: upload 200, cross-user read 200 with the row, cross-user create 200.

## Classification

Security/permission-separation gap, **P1** for multi-tenant use. The default dev seed is not a
tenant boundary; the use-case catalogs are.

items.title: RFC: App Data — persistent CRUD storage for Mako apps
items.body:
# RFC: App Data — a provisioned serverless database per app

> **v2** — reworked after design discussion. v1 proposed a records store in Mako's MongoDB; we decided against putting app data in Mongo. App data now lives in a **provisioned serverless SQL database**, registered as a regular Mako connection, with the storage backend **configurable** (Mako-managed by default, BYO later).

## Problem

Mako apps are read-only data products. They can query workspace data through bindings, but they have nowhere to **write**: no stored edits, no form submissions, no trackers, no approval queues — nothing whose point is creating and updating records. The only "state" story is URL params, because the app iframe is an opaque-origin sandbox with no cookies or localStorage.

**First principle:** an app platform needs a data layer. Apps should be able to do full CRUD — like any real app — without opening a write path into customer *analytic* warehouses (which stay read-only by design) and without commingling tenant data in Mako's control-plane MongoDB.

## Core idea

**Every app gets its own database.** Mako provisions a serverless SQL database (behind a provider interface), stores only a pointer + credentials (encrypted, existing AES-256 utilities), and registers it as a **regular Mako connection** scoped to the workspace.

Why this shape wins:

1. **Physical isolation.** One tenant's app data is in its own database. The blast radius of any query is the app's own data — which is what makes full SQL CRUD safe to offer at all.
2. **Queryability for free.** Because the store is a normal Mako connection, app data is immediately usable by the entire existing stack — consoles, data bindings, notebooks, dbt, the explorer sidebar, `sql_inspect_table` — with **zero new query machinery**. "Can I join app data with warehouse data?" becomes a client-side/dbt exercise, not a feature to build.
3. **Configurable by construction.** The provisioner is an interface. Mako-managed (default, zero setup) and BYO (workspace admin supplies their own Neon/Postgres/D1) are just two implementations that emit the same connection object. Data-ownership story: it's a standard SQL database; export or take over the credentials.
4. **No new schema system.** Schema = SQL tables. The agent (or user) runs `CREATE TABLE`; existing introspection documents it.
5. **Nothing in Mongo but a pointer.** Control plane and tenant data stay separated.

## Goals

- Apps can **create, read, update, delete** rows in their own database from app code.
- App data is **independent of the app definition**: survives edits, publishes, version restores (snapshots never include data).
- Data is **workspace-scoped and app-scoped**, enforced server-side; the sandbox never holds credentials.
- **Anyone who can use the app** can read/write its data (using ≠ editing); **agents/MCP** get first-class access; granular rules ride on the permissions system later.
- Storage backend is **configurable per workspace**: Mako-managed default now, BYO fast-follow.

## Non-goals (v1)

- **No writes to customer analytic warehouses.** The read-only boundary (`checkPreviewQuerySafety`, no `query:write` scope) is untouched — the app DB is a separate, Mako-provisioned resource.
- **No anonymous public writes.** `/share/:token` stays read-only; public form submissions are a follow-up with an abuse-control story.
- **No cross-app or cross-workspace queries** from app code.

## Design

### Provisioning

```ts
interface AppDatabaseProvisioner {
  provision(workspaceId, appId): Promise<AppDbRef>;   // idempotent; lazy on first write/DDL
  destroy(ref): Promise<void>;                        // on app delete
  usage(ref): Promise<{ bytes: number; rows?: number }>;
}
```

- Implementations: one managed provider to start (see Open Question 1: Neon vs Cloudflare D1 vs Turso), `BYOPostgres` later.
- Granularity depends on provider economics: **Postgres → one database per workspace, one schema per app** (search_path enforced server-side; drop schema on app delete). **D1/Turso → one database per app** (cheap thousands-of-DBs model).
- Provisioning is **lazy**: an app that never writes never allocates anything.
- The resulting `AppDbRef` is surfaced as a workspace connection (badged "App Data"), so it appears in the explorer and is queryable everywhere connections are.

### Write path & SDK

All traffic transits `postMessage → host → Mako API → app DB` (the iframe can never hold credentials — this is transport necessity, not a policy choice). The synthetic `@mako/app-sdk` gains:

```ts
// Escape hatch: full SQL against the app's OWN database (parameterized only)
const db = useAppDb();
await db.query("INSERT INTO submissions (name, status) VALUES ($1, $2)", [name, "open"]);
const rows = await db.query("SELECT * FROM submissions WHERE status = $1", ["open"]);

// Sugar for the 90% case and agent-generated code (compiles to SQL server-side)
const { rows, loading, insert, update, remove, refetch } =
  useTable("submissions", { where: { status: "open" }, orderBy: "created_at desc", limit: 100 });
```

- New bridge messages (`dbQuery` / `dbResult` / `dataChanged`) using the existing `requestId`/pending-map pattern.
- Parameterized statements only; per-(user, app) rate limits; statement timeout; result row caps.
- **DDL vs DML split**: DML (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) for anyone who can *use* the app; DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP) for app **editors** and the agent — schema changes are part of building the app, data changes are part of using it.
- Realtime: `app.data.changed {appId, table}` event → hosts poke booted iframes → hooks refetch (same mechanism as `app.updated`).

### Hosts

| Host | Identity | v1 posture |
|---|---|---|
| `AppRenderer` (editor/viewer tab) | session | read + write |
| `AppPreviewPage` (`mpt_` token) | preview token | read-only (tokens are documented read/execute-only; writability would need an explicit capability bit) |
| `PublicAppViewer` (`/share/:token`) | share token | read-only; hooks expose `readOnly: true` so apps hide edit affordances |

### REST API

```
POST /api/workspaces/:wid/apps/:id/db/query     # parameterized SQL, DML for canRead, DDL for canManage
GET  /api/workspaces/:wid/apps/:id/db           # ref, usage, provisioning state
```

Inherits the existing auth + workspace middleware and resource ACL on the apps router. Reads can also flow through **normal data bindings** against the app-data connection — no special path needed.

### Agent / MCP

- The app-data connection is visible to existing tools (`sql_list_tables`, `sql_inspect_table`, `sql_execute_query`), so agents explore it like any source.
- New `app_db_query` tool for writes/DDL (the agent scaffolds tables and seeds data when building an app). Must be classified in the MCP bridge policy **and** the agent tool tier registry (unclassified tools are silently dead).
- Apps skill updated so agent-built apps use `useAppDb`/`useTable` instead of inventing state hacks.
- Note: this introduces the first deliberate write capability into the MCP surface — scope it (`app-data:write`) rather than widening the existing read-only stance.

### Lifecycle & versioning

- Provision lazily; **destroy on app delete** (with a grace window / soft-delete before drop).
- `buildAppSnapshot` / `applyAppSnapshot` never touch app data — restore, publish, unpublish have no effect on the database (precedent: `dataBindings[].cache`).
- Duplicating an app duplicates schema, not data (open question 3).

### Limits & safety

- Per-app quota (e.g. 1 GB default, provider-enforced where possible; `usage()` surfaced in the editor).
- Parameterized-only statements; deny multi-statement batches, `ATTACH`/`COPY`/extension loading per provider.
- Statement timeout + row caps on the query path; per-(user, app) write rate limits.
- Isolation: separate DB per app where the provider makes that cheap; on shared-Postgres granularity, per-app schema + enforced `search_path` (per-schema roles as a hardening follow-up).

## Phasing

- **Phase 1 — Managed provider + write path**: provisioner interface + one managed implementation; `/db/query` endpoint; bridge + `useAppDb`/`useTable`; DDL/DML permission split; realtime invalidation; connection registration (explorer + bindings can read it); agent tool + skill docs; quotas.
- **Phase 2 — Configurability & product surface**: BYO backend (admin-supplied Postgres); data browser in the app editor; export; per-table permission rules via the permissions system.
- **Phase 3 — Openings**: opt-in anonymous submissions on public shares (forms/surveys); scheduled replication of app tables into the customer warehouse via `DestinationWriter` for dbt-everywhere; branch/copy app data alongside app duplication.

## Open questions

1. **Managed provider**: Neon (serverless Postgres; scale-to-zero; full PG so every existing driver/dbt path works; per-workspace DB + per-app schema) vs Cloudflare D1 (already a supported Mako driver, same stack as `cf:deploy`, cheap DB-per-app; SQLite semantics) vs Turso (libSQL, built for thousands of per-tenant DBs). Leaning Neon for Postgres compatibility; D1 if we want to stay all-Cloudflare.
2. **Granularity vs provider**: confirm per-workspace-DB/per-app-schema (Postgres) or per-app-DB (SQLite-family) once the provider is picked.
3. **App duplication**: copy schema only, or schema + data?
4. **BYO trust model**: when the admin supplies the database, do we still enforce the DDL/DML split, or is it their problem?

## Prior art

- **PR #669** (closed, unmerged): KV-only `useStorage` in Mongo. Superseded by this design; a `useStorage` convenience hook can still ship as sugar over a KV table in the app DB.
- **Apps platform PRD** (`docs/mako-apps-platform-prd.md`): lists an "app-scoped data endpoint" as a gap; this RFC fills it with a database rather than an endpoint.
- **`dataBindings[].cache`**: the established pattern for server-owned, non-versioned app state.
- **`public-live-query.service.ts`**: the safety envelope (opt-in flag, rate limits, TTL cache, timeouts) to copy for Phase 3 public writes.

items.title: Tracking: runbook for the workshop
items.body:
Runbook for getting the lab and the TALXIS toolchain ready for the workshop. **Run the lanes top to bottom. A step starts only when its gate is ticked.** Every step links an issue or PR whose comments contain implementation notes for the agent session that does it. Lockstep steps are marked 🔗. Releases are fine at any time, including hotfixes during the workshop.

**Released so far:**
- platform-metadata v0.13.1
- tools-devkit-build **v1.10.0** (#133 `[PluginStep]`, #136)
- tools-devkit-templates **v1.25.3** (pins SDK 1.10.0)
- tools-cli **v1.22.0** (#221 env-type guard, device-code fallback in `profile create --url`)

Codespaces pick them up on their next start.

items.title: KF-RD-GENAI-STACK-2026-001 — Converged AI systems R&D
items.body:
# KF-RD-GENAI-STACK-2026-001

## Purpose
Durable research ledger for the methodical dissection of the 2026 GenAI stack and adjacent systems, followed by scientific/work-domain parallelisation and whole-system convergence into KEYFLOWOS / KEY.

This is **research and architectural memory**, not implementation authority. Production code remains untouched until findings are converged, dependency-ordered, and separately authorized for implementation.

## Required method for every subject
1. Technical dissection: architecture, primitives, algorithms, APIs, state, persistence, execution lifecycle, concurrency, failure/retry/cancellation, security, tenancy, observability, evaluation, scaling, latency, cost, DX, extensibility, licensing, known failure modes.
2. Source inspection where code is open.
3. Microscopic comparison against live KEYFLOWOS.
4. Scientific parallelisation: neuroscience, physiology, cybernetics/control theory, information theory, graph theory, distributed systems, statistics, OR, ecology/evolution, safety engineering, etc., but only where the mechanism is structurally transferable.
5. Work/operational parallelisation: medicine, aviation, finance/accounting, logistics, industrial safety, incident response, organizations, command-and-control, etc.
6. Mechanism extraction.
7. KEY/KEYFLOWOS hypothesis.
8. Experiment + measurable proof obligation.
9. Disposition: ADOPT / ADAPT / ABSORB / MERGE / REPLACE / REMOVE / BENCHMARK / WATCH / REJECT.
10. Hold findings for convergence; do not cargo-cult dependencies.

## Dual targets
Every useful finding is assessed for:
- KEY / KEYFLOWOS runtime.
- The autonomous development machinery building KEYFLOWOS (Claude Code / control plane / repo intelligence / review loops).

## Completion standard
The programme is not complete until individual subjects are researched, cross-domain mechanisms extracted, contradictions/duplicates identified, uncertain claims experimentally resolved, and the results converged into a small set of canonical architectural primitives with explicit invariants and proof obligations.

## Inventory
Layer 1: OpenAI/GPT; Anthropic/Claude; Gemini; Llama; DeepSeek; Qwen.
Layer 2: vLLM; Ollama; llama.cpp; Groq; Bedrock; Vertex AI.
Layer 3: LangChain; LangGraph; LlamaIndex; CrewAI; AutoGen; Pydantic AI.
Layer 4: OpenAI embeddings; Cohere; Voyage; Jina; BGE; Nomic.
Layer 5: Pinecone; Qdrant; Weaviate; Milvus; Chroma; pgvector.
Layer 6: Hugging Face; PEFT/LoRA; Unsloth; Axolotl; TRL; LLaMA-Factory.
Layer 7: DSPy; Instructor; Outlines; Guidance; BAML; provider structured outputs.
Layer 8: MCP; native function calling; A2A; computer/browser use; Composio; Arcade.
Layer 9: LangSmith; Langfuse; Ragas; DeepEval; Phoenix; W&B Weave.
Layer 10: NeMo Guardrails; Guardrails AI; Llama Guard; Lakera; Presidio; Rebuff.

The inventory expands when adjacent/superior systems are discovered.

## Progress
- R&D-01A OpenAI/GPT: first-pass technical dissection completed; findings held for Layer-1 convergence.
- R&D-01B Anthropic/Claude: active.

## R&D-01A — OpenAI/GPT holding findings
- Capability-based cognitive scheduling instead of model-name routing.
- Responses-style typed cognitive event streams should map underneath KEY's own lifecycle, not replace Cortex.
- Model tool selection is evidence/intent, never business-action authority.
- Machine-facing outputs should be schema-first; human presentation should not be reparsed into state.
- Hierarchical/deferred capability discovery ("capability paging") is high-value for KEY's large tool/connector surface.
- Prompt/context layout should be designed for cache locality: stable constitution -> stable business context -> semi-stable genome/session -> dynamic turn.
- Provider conversation state is ephemeral execution state, never canonical KEY memory.
- Classify AI work as realtime / interactive / background / batch / scheduled / event-triggered.
- Create a capability/lifecycle-aware model catalog.
- Current live repo gap: OpenAI path still uses Chat Completions and direct OpenAI calls exist outside the model gateway (embeddings/vision/voice/document paths); provider boundary is not yet fully converged.

## Continuity rule
Each completed subject should add a durable comment here containing:
- source-backed findings,
- current KEYFLOWOS comparison,
- science/work parallels,
- extracted mechanisms,
- candidate experiments,
- disposition,
- interactions/contradictions with earlier findings,
- implementation implications held for convergence.

At each layer boundary, publish a layer-convergence comment before proceeding to the next layer.

# Phase26 — Support Hub & Conversation Management

**Implementation-ready specification. All D1–D40 decisions and amendments are ratified; the founder confirmed the testing approach.**

Support Hub is one cohesive Asym surface with shared native CRM context and correctly authorized owner actions. This specification preserves the complete email/intake/work lifecycle, private collaboration, drafts and reading preferences, contextual guidance, safe file reading and recoverable Unwanted/future-mail holding journeys.

**Start with the user-story book**, then follow its stable US26/REQ26/AC26 identifiers into the detailed requirement volumes. The glossary fixes domain language; OpenSpec carries observable behavior, design and the unchecked implementation/qualification checklist. The source trace records every captured section's authority and disposition.

The full package contains **217 independently verifiable user stories, 2,210 detailed requirement definitions, 717 main OpenSpec scenarios, and all additional exact proof/operating-control suites**. It covers **all 40 ratified decisions**, including D27-C, D29-X01 and every accepted correction. Numerical limits, state/audience/source rules, failure recovery and release gates remain binding.

**Email Studio/P17** owns governed reusable content, canonical authoring and whole-message preparation. **P6** owns actual communication, provider evidence and recovery. **Support** owns human work, source-specific intent and private drafting; canonical intake owns receiving and held-mail decisions. CRM and giving/care domains retain their own truth, permissions and mutations. These seams are specified throughout the requirements, not left as integration assumptions.

**Confirmed proof approach:** real authenticated Support/API and canonical intake/job boundaries on disposable local Supabase; focused actual database permission/concurrency/migration proof; and full Playwright journeys on that same backend. Existing frameworks are reused and real-provider qualification stays separate.

items.body:
## AI Engineer 能力地圖：Frame × 關鍵字

以下以每個 frame 作為領域；每個關鍵字一列，欄位固定為一句話理解、概念、技術、實作、情境、注意；「一句話理解」以 Full Stack 工程師熟悉的系統開發視角說明。

### Data Engineering

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETL / ELT | 像後端資料搬運管線：抽取資料、整理格式，再送進分析系統。 | 把來源資料可靠地送到分析層；ETL先轉換、ELT先落地再轉換。 | 批次/增量、CDC、schema evolution、Spark/dbt。 | 以Airflow排程、dbt轉換、資料品質檢查與重跑機制落地。 | 報表、數據同步、資料湖到倉庫。 | 避免全量重跑；處理重複、遲到資料、PII與schema變更。 |
| Data Warehouse | 專門給報表與分析查詢的集中式資料庫。 | 面向分析的集中式資料儲存，重視一致性與查詢效能。 | 星型模型、分區、columnar storage、OLAP。 | 建立raw/staging/mart分層與維度/事實表。 | BI、KPI、跨來源報表。 | 不要把交易庫直接當分析庫；控管成本與資料新鮮度。 |
| Data Lake / Lakehouse | 像大型物件儲存倉庫，但加上可查詢、版本與治理能力。 | 保留大量原始資料並兼顧治理與分析能力。 | Object storage、Parquet、Delta/Iceberg、schema-on-read。 | 以bronze/silver/gold分層，設定catalog、partition與compact。 | 半結構化資料、ML訓練、歷史留存。 | 小檔案與無治理會拖垮查詢；需管理版本、權限與生命週期。 |
| Streaming / Real-time | 把資料當事件即時處理，類似 WebSocket 或 queue consumer。 | 資料事件產生後即時處理，而非等待批次窗口。 | Kafka/PubSub、Flink/Spark Streaming、watermark、幂等。 | 設計topic/schema、consumer group、checkpoint與DLQ。 | 即時告警、推薦、即時儀表板。 | 至少一次不等於不重複；處理順序、背壓、遲到事件與重放。 |
| Data Modeling | 替資料設計可長期維護的 schema、關聯與統計口徑。 | 把業務實體、關係與指標轉成可查詢且可演進的結構。 | 正規化/反正規化、維度建模、SCD、data contract。 | 先定義grain，再建立主鍵、外鍵、指標與欄位字典。 | 跨團隊共用資料、報表與特徵。 | grain不清會造成重複計算；避免只為當下報表硬編模型。 |
| Data Quality & Governance | 替資料加上測試、ownership、權限與可追溯性。 | 確保資料正確、完整、及時、可追溯且有人負責。 | 契約測試、expectations、lineage、catalog、SLA。 | 在pipeline加入schema、null、範圍、freshness與異常告警。 | 重要報表、監管資料、ML輸入。 | 品質規則要可執行；告警過多會被忽略，需訂責任人與處置流程。 |
| Orchestration | 像 CI/CD workflow，負責安排資料任務的順序、重試與排程。 | 管理資料工作流的依賴、重試、排程與可觀測性。 | DAG、Airflow/Dagster、sensor、backfill、retry。 | 任務保持冪等，設定timeout、重試、依賴與失敗通知。 | 多步ETL、每日報表、模型pipeline。 | 不要把業務邏輯塞進排程器；避免隱性依賴與無限重試。 |

### RAG / LLM Application

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture | 把 ingestion、搜尋、LLM 與 API 拆成有清楚邊界的服務。 | 定義RAG元件如何串接、資料流如何走，以及同步/非同步邊界。 | Retriever-generator pipeline、API gateway、cache、queue。 | 拆 ingestion、retrieval、generation、evaluation 與 serving。 | 企業知識問答、客服、文件搜尋。 | 先定義延遲、成本、權限與失敗降級，再選框架。 |
| Chunking | 把長文件切成模型搜尋得到、又看得懂的小段落。 | 把文件切成適合檢索與模型上下文的片段。 | 固定長度、語意切分、recursive splitter、overlap。 | 依標題/段落切分，保留metadata並用檢索指標調整大小。 | 長文件問答、規章與技術文件。 | 切太小失去上下文，切太大降低召回；不要切斷表格與程式碼。 |
| Embedding | 把文字轉成可比較相似度的數字向量。 | 將文字轉成向量，讓語意相近內容在向量空間靠近。 | Transformer embedding、cosine similarity、批次embedding。 | 固定模型與版本，建立向量索引並記錄embedding model。 | 語意搜尋、相似案例、RAG召回。 | 模型換版需重建索引；多語、領域詞與向量維度要驗證。 |
| Vector DB | 替 embedding 建索引，讓系統能快速做語意搜尋。 | 儲存與查詢向量及其metadata的資料庫。 | HNSW/IVF、ANN、top-k、filter、Qdrant/pgvector/Milvus。 | 建立collection、索引、metadata filter與刪除/更新流程。 | 大量文件的語意檢索。 | top-k不是品質保證；注意索引更新、租戶隔離與查詢成本。 |
| Metadata Filtering | 像 SQL WHERE，先用權限、租戶或日期縮小搜尋範圍。 | 先用結構化條件縮小可檢索範圍，再做語意搜尋。 | 欄位filter、ACL filter、tenant_id、時間/版本條件。 | 把權限與來源metadata寫入chunk，檢索時強制套用。 | 依部門、產品、日期、權限搜尋。 | filter不能由模型自由決定；缺metadata會造成越權或漏召回。 |
| Hybrid Search | 同時跑關鍵字搜尋和語意搜尋，再合併結果。 | 結合關鍵字精確匹配與向量語意匹配。 | BM25、dense retrieval、rank fusion、RRF。 | 並行查詢兩路召回後融合、去重並評估權重。 | 專有名詞、編號與自然語言混合查詢。 | 只用向量容易漏掉ID/術語；融合權重需用資料驗證。 |
| Reranker | 像搜尋結果的第二輪排序器，把真正相關的內容往前排。 | 對初步召回結果重新排序，提升前幾筆相關性。 | Cross-encoder、Cohere rerank、top-N reranking。 | 先取較大的candidate pool，再對前N筆重排。 | 召回很多但答案常不在前幾筆。 | 會增加延遲與成本；不要把reranker當作權限層。 |
| Query Rewriting | 把使用者模糊的問題改寫成更容易查到資料的查詢。 | 把模糊、口語或多輪問題改寫成更適合檢索的查詢。 | Query expansion、multi-query、HyDE、conversation rewrite。 | 保留原問題，產生候選查詢並記錄改寫結果。 | 追問、省略主詞、跨語言與複雜問題。 | 改寫可能改變原意；需防止注入與錯誤擴張。 |
| Evaluation | 像單元測試與回歸測試，但測的是 AI 回答品質。 | 用可重複的案例與指標衡量檢索和生成品質。 | Recall@k、MRR、faithfulness、answer relevancy、LLM judge。 | 建立golden set、版本化評測並在CI執行回歸測試。 | prompt、模型、chunk策略比較。 | 單一分數會掩蓋失敗類型；要分檢索、生成與安全評估。 |
| Faithfulness | 檢查答案是否真的有文件證據支持。 | 答案是否能被提供的上下文支持，而非模型自行捏造。 | Citation checking、NLI、LLM-as-judge、groundedness。 | 要求引用來源，逐句比對claim與context並設拒答門檻。 | 法規、客服、內部知識問答。 | 有引用不代表真的支持；避免把judge分數當絕對真值。 |
| Hallucination | 模型講得很像真的，但內容其實沒有依據。 | 模型產生與證據不符或不存在的內容。 | Grounding、temperature control、answer abstention、fact check。 | 無證據時拒答，輸出引用與信心，記錄錯誤案例回歸。 | 資料不完整或問題超出知識庫。 | 降低temperature無法根治；需改善召回與輸出驗證。 |
| Failure Modes | 列出系統會怎麼壞，並預先設計偵測、降級與復原。 | 系統在資料、檢索、模型、工具或網路異常下的失敗型態。 | Failure taxonomy、chaos test、timeout、retry、DLQ。 | 建立錯誤分類、fallback、告警與可重現測試案例。 | 上線前演練與事故分析。 | 只測happy path不夠；重試可能放大流量與費用。 |

### Agent

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Workflow | 像後端狀態機，把 Agent 任務拆成可控制的步驟。 | 把Agent任務拆成可追蹤、可重試、可控的步驟。 | State machine、DAG、LangGraph、workflow engine。 | 明確定義節點輸入輸出、轉移條件與終止條件。 | 多步研究、客服處理、資料操作。 | 避免讓模型自行決定所有流程；限制迴圈與最大步數。 |
| Tool Calling | 讓模型用結構化參數呼叫 API，而不是只產生文字。 | 讓模型以結構化參數呼叫外部工具完成工作。 | Function calling、JSON schema、tool registry。 | 驗證參數、套用權限、執行工具並把結果回傳模型。 | 查詢API、寄信、寫入資料庫。 | 工具呼叫等同權限操作；需白名單、審計與人工核准。 |
| State | 保存 Agent 做到哪裡、拿到什麼結果，以及下一步要做什麼。 | 保存Agent在多步任務中的上下文、結果與目前階段。 | State schema、checkpoint、短期/長期記憶。 | 用明確schema儲存狀態，支援重試、恢復與版本遷移。 | 長流程、多輪對話、非同步任務。 | 不要把所有對話無限塞進prompt；避免狀態污染與競態。 |
| Planning | 讓 Agent 先拆任務再執行，但每一步仍要驗證。 | 先決定子任務與執行順序，再逐步完成目標。 | ReAct、plan-and-execute、task decomposition。 | 限制計畫深度，逐步驗證工具結果並允許重新規劃。 | 研究、複合查詢、跨系統流程。 | 計畫不是事實；每一步都需驗證，並防止無限重新規劃。 |
| Guardrails | 像 middleware 與 policy layer，限制模型與工具能做什麼。 | 在輸入、工具、輸出各階段限制Agent可做的事。 | Policy engine、schema validation、content filter、allowlist。 | 建立前置/後置檢查，違規時拒絕、修正或轉人工。 | 高風險自動化、金融、客服。 | 只做輸出過濾不夠；工具層和資料層也要防護。 |
| Human-in-the-loop | 高風險動作先停住，交給人核准後才繼續。 | 在高風險或不確定步驟由人審核、接管或核准。 | Approval gate、confidence threshold、escalation。 | 設計待審佇列、審核理由、逾時與回滾流程。 | 付款、刪除、對外發信、敏感回答。 | 人工介入點要可量化；避免所有案件都卡在人工作業。 |
| Structured Output | 要求模型回傳符合 JSON Schema 的資料，方便程式接續處理。 | 要求模型輸出可被程式可靠解析的固定結構。 | JSON schema、Pydantic、constrained decoding。 | 解析後做schema與業務規則驗證，失敗則修復或重試。 | API回應、分類、工作流節點。 | 格式正確不代表內容正確；限制欄位長度與注入內容。 |
| Evaluation | 像單元測試與回歸測試，但測的是 AI 回答品質。 | 用可重複的案例與指標衡量檢索和生成品質。 | Recall@k、MRR、faithfulness、answer relevancy、LLM judge。 | 建立golden set、版本化評測並在CI執行回歸測試。 | prompt、模型、chunk策略比較。 | 單一分數會掩蓋失敗類型；要分檢索、生成與安全評估。 |

### Multi-tenant

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Multi-tenant Architecture | 同一套後端服務多家公司，但每家的資料與資源必須隔離。 | 同一平台服務多個租戶，同時共享效率與隔離安全。 | Shared service、tenant context、quota、policy。 | 每個request注入tenant context，所有資料與快取操作強制帶租戶。 | SaaS型AI平台。 | 租戶邊界必須端到端驗證，不能只靠前端參數。 |

| Fault Tolerance | 部分元件壞掉時，系統仍能降級服務並自動復原。 | Fault Tolerance在系統架構中的核心問題與設計邊界。 | queue、cache、事件、限流與容錯；以Fault Tolerance相關指標驗證取捨。 | 在系統架構流程中建立可測試、可監控的Fault Tolerance模組。 | 高流量與非同步系統中的Fault Tolerance使用情境。 | 注意一致性、故障邊界、背壓與觀測；需用測試、權限與告警避免失控。 |
| Horizontal Scaling | 增加更多相同服務實例來處理更高流量。 | Horizontal Scaling在系統架構中的核心問題與設計邊界。 | queue、cache、事件、限流與容錯；以Horizontal Scaling相關指標驗證取捨。 | 在系統架構流程中建立可測試、可監控的Horizontal Scaling模組。 | 高流量與非同步系統中的Horizontal Scaling使用情境。 | 注意一致性、故障邊界、背壓與觀測；需用測試、權限與告警避免失控。 |
| Observability | 把 metrics、logs、traces 串起來，看懂線上系統發生什麼。 | 讓團隊知道系統發生什麼、品質如何、成本多少。 | Metrics、logs、traces、dashboards、alerts。 | 關聯request id、tenant、model、prompt版本與結果指標。 | 線上除錯、SLA與容量規劃。 | 避免記錄原始敏感prompt；指標需能對應行動。 |
| Distributed Systems | 多個服務與節點共同完成工作，因此要處理網路、同步與一致性問題。 | Distributed Systems在系統架構中的核心問題與設計邊界。 | queue、cache、事件、限流與容錯；以Distributed Systems相關指標驗證取捨。 | 在系統架構流程中建立可測試、可監控的Distributed Systems模組。 | 高流量與非同步系統中的Distributed Systems使用情境。 | 注意一致性、故障邊界、背壓與觀測；需用測試、權限與告警避免失控。 |

> 來源：Miro board 的 10 個 frame；內容以 Full Stack 工程師理解 AI 工程能力地圖為目標整理。

## AI 系統從建置到上線：三段流程

閱讀順序只有三段：**先準備資料 → 再處理使用者請求 → 最後用線上結果持續改善**。底部三項是每個階段都必須具備的系統能力。

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph PREP["A. 事前準備：把資料變成 AI 可用的知識"]
    direction LR
    DE["1. Data Engineering<br/>收集、清理、治理資料"]
    DS["2. Data Science<br/>分析資料、定義指標與特徵"]
    ML["3. ML 基礎<br/>選模型、Embedding 與推論方式"]
    KB[("可檢索知識庫<br/>Chunks + Metadata + Vectors")]
    DE --> DS --> ML --> KB
  end

  subgraph REQUEST["B. 線上請求：使用者問問題時，系統實際怎麼跑"]
    direction LR
    USER["使用者 / 前端"] --> API["API 接收問題"]
    API --> RAG["4. RAG / LLM Application<br/>找資料、排序、組 Prompt"]
    RAG --> NEED{"需要執行動作？"}
    NEED -->|否| ANSWER["LLM 產生答案"]
    NEED -->|是| AGENT["5. Agent<br/>規劃步驟、呼叫工具、保存狀態"]
    AGENT --> ANSWER
    ANSWER --> USER
  end

  KB -->|提供相關資料| RAG

  subgraph IMPROVE["C. 上線後：觀察結果並持續改善"]
    direction LR
    OBS["6. Production AI / Observability<br/>記錄品質、延遲、成本與錯誤"]
    EVAL["7. LLM Evaluation<br/>Golden Dataset、Judge、Faithfulness"]
    FIX["修正資料 / Prompt / 模型 / 流程"]
    OBS --> EVAL --> FIX
  end

  ANSWER -->|留下 Trace 與 Feedback| OBS
  FIX -->|重新發佈| RAG
  FIX -->|補資料與品質規則| DE

  CROSS["所有階段共同要求<br/>8. Multi-tenant：租戶與資料隔離<br/>9. AI Security / Reliability：權限、PII、Guardrails<br/>10. Architecture：Queue、Cache、Scaling、Fault Tolerance"]
```

items.title: Epic: Wellyboot BI, a BI dashboard builder for Puddle data
items.body:
## Vision

Puddle cleans data in the browser. Wellyboot BI shows it. A dataset curated in Puddle is loaded into Wellyboot BI, where you pick a data source, drag fields into a chart, arrange several charts on a canvas, and save the result as a dashboard. A dashboard can be shared with a unique link, so anyone who has it can open the dashboard and query the data behind it, and any single chart can be published as HTML to embed in a website.

The two apps should feel like one family: the same design system, the same stack, the same plain-word tone, and the same promise that nothing leaves your browser unless you choose to publish it.

## Goals

- A Power BI-like authoring experience in the browser: a data source picker, a field list, field wells (axis, values, legend, filters), and a canvas of visuals.
- Bar, line and pie charts first, built on a chart model that grows to tables, area, scatter, KPI cards, donuts, stacked bars and maps without reworking the editor.
- Dashboards that hold several visuals over one or more Puddle data sources, with layout, filters and slicers, saved and reopened like Puddle projects.
- Sharing by unique URL: a published dashboard is read-only, queryable by anyone with the link, and the link can be revoked.
- Publishing a single chart to HTML that can be embedded in a website, either as a self-contained snapshot or as a live embed.
- Local-first authoring: everything up to sharing works offline in the browser on DuckDB-WASM, as Puddle does. The server only enters when something is published.
- Every feature ships with its tests, as in Puddle: unit tests next to the code, engine tests on real DuckDB-WASM, and a Playwright test of the user-facing flow.

## Non-goals (for this epic)

- Replacing Puddle's cleaning steps: Wellyboot BI does not transform data beyond aggregating, filtering and sorting it for a chart. Fix the data in Puddle.
- Connecting to live databases, warehouses or SaaS APIs. The data source is a Puddle dataset (a file Puddle exported, or one Puddle publishes to Wellyboot BI).
- Multi-tenant accounts, teams, roles and row-level security. Wellyboot BI is self-hosted and single-tenant: an author (or a few) publishes; the public reads.
- Scheduled refreshes, alerts, subscriptions or email delivery.
- A paginated "report" document format distinct from a dashboard. In this epic a report and a dashboard are the same thing; see Open questions.
- A native mobile app. The web app should work on a phone, but is designed for a desktop browser.

## Key concepts

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Data source (dataset) | One table of curated rows with a known schema, exported from a Puddle Output node (CSV, Parquet, JSON or NDJSON) and loaded into Wellyboot BI. It carries provenance where Puddle supplies it: project name, Output node, export time, the source fingerprint (Puddle's `headHash`) and the quality rules that passed. |
| Field | One column of a data source, typed as number, text, date/time or boolean (from DuckDB's types, as in Puddle's `ColumnSchema`). |
| Query | What a visual asks of a data source: the fields to group by, the summaries to compute (sum, average, count, distinct count, min, max), filters, sort order and a row limit. A query compiles to one DuckDB `SELECT`, and nothing else in the app writes SQL. |
| Visual (chart) | A query plus a chart spec: the chart type, which query columns go on which encoding (x, y, colour, size, tooltip), and formatting (title, axis labels, number format, colours). A visual's spec compiles to a Vega-Lite spec for rendering. |
| Canvas | The grid where visuals are placed and resized, in the spirit of Puddle's node canvas but a layout grid, not a graph. |
| Dashboard (report) | A named document holding data source references, visuals, their layout on the canvas, and dashboard-level filters and slicers. Saved as `.wellyboot.json`, versioned and migrated like Puddle's `.puddle.json`. |
| Slicer | A dashboard-level control (a list, a range, a date picker) bound to one field that filters every visual over that field. |
| Share link | A unique, unguessable URL to a published copy of a dashboard. Whoever has it can open the dashboard read-only and run its queries, including changing slicers. It is scoped, revocable and rate-limited; see the security model. |
| Embed | One visual published as HTML: either a self-contained file with its data inlined (a snapshot) or a small page that loads the visual live from Wellyboot BI through an embed token. |
| Publish | The explicit act of sending a dashboard (and the datasets it needs) from the browser to a Wellyboot BI server so that it can be shared or embedded. Nothing is published without it. |

## Architecture overview

Wellyboot BI is a monorepo with three packages. It departs from Puddle's single-package layout because Wellyboot BI has a server, and the model schemas must be shared between the browser and the server.

```
WellybootBI/
  apps/web/        The Wellyboot BI web app (Vite, React, TypeScript). Local-first on DuckDB-WASM.
  apps/server/     The Wellyboot BI server (Node, TypeScript): publishing, share links, embed tokens, dataset files.
  packages/shared/ Zod schemas for datasets, queries, visuals, dashboards and the server API; format versions and migrations.
```

The web app follows Puddle's layering, with the same names where the job is the same:

- `engine/`: DuckDB-WASM in a Web Worker behind a typed client with priorities and cancellation, after Puddle's `src/engine/`.
- `model/`: the dashboard document as Zod schemas, with edits, undo and redo, after Puddle's `src/model/`.
- `compiler/`: the only place SQL is generated (query model to `SELECT`), quoting through one `sql.ts` as Puddle does in `src/compiler/sql.ts`; and the chart compiler (visual spec to Vega-Lite).
- `datasets/`: loading Puddle exports into DuckDB, the dataset catalogue, provenance and profiles.
- `visuals/`, `canvas/`, `dashboard/`: the editor, after Puddle's `src/steps/`, `src/canvas/` and `src/inspector/`.
- `persistence/`: IndexedDB autosave, `.wellyboot.json` export and import, migrations, after Puddle's `src/persistence/`.
- `publish/`: talking to the server; `viewer/` and `embed/`: the read-only entry points.
- `design-system/` and `ui/`: Puddle's tokens, components and formatting, vendored the same way Puddle vendors them.

Queries run in the browser. In the editor, the viewer and live embeds alike, DuckDB-WASM reads the dataset (local bytes in the editor; Parquet served by the Wellyboot BI server, by HTTP range request, in the viewer) and runs the compiled `SELECT`. The server never executes SQL sent by the public, which keeps its attack surface to serving files and checking tokens. Server-side query is left as an open question for datasets too large to send to a browser.

The server is small: a Node 22 TypeScript service with SQLite for metadata (dashboards, datasets, tokens, usage counters) and a directory of dataset files on a volume (S3-compatible storage later). It is deployed as a second service next to the nginx image in Docker Compose, behind the same Cloudflare Tunnel pattern Puddle uses (`deploy/README.md` in Puddle).

## How Wellyboot BI talks to Puddle

What Puddle offers today, from its code:

- Puddle is a static site with no server and no API. "Nothing leaves your browser. Projects save the steps, not the data" (`README.md`). The deploy is nginx serving files (`Dockerfile`, `deploy/README.md`).
- Curated data leaves Puddle only as an export from an Output node: CSV, Parquet, JSON, NDJSON, Excel or the clipboard, written by DuckDB's `COPY ... TO` and downloaded (`src/compiler/export.ts`, `src/export/run.ts`, `docs/exporting.md`). Delivery is a pluggable function, `Delivery = (blob, fileName, format) => Promise<void>` in `src/export/run.ts`.
- Puddle's project file (`.puddle.json`) and recipes (`.puddle-recipe.json`) hold sources, steps and rules but no rows (`src/model/schema.ts`, `src/recipes/recipe.ts`, `src/persistence/shareable.ts`). Sync to GitHub Gist or Google Drive pushes that same data-free file (`src/sync/file.ts`). None of these can feed a dashboard.
- Puddle knows a dataset's schema (`detectedSchema`, an array of `{ name, type }` in `src/model/schema.ts`), a fingerprint of each source (`headHash`), and the quality rules that passed (`src/report/build.ts`). This is the provenance Wellyboot BI wants to show next to a data source.
- Puddle reads CSV, JSON and Parquet from any https address whose server sends CORS headers, Parquet by range request (`src/sources/url.ts`, `docs/sources.md`). So a dataset published to Wellyboot BI can be read back into Puddle for the next round of cleaning, if the Wellyboot BI server sends CORS headers.

So the integration is in two steps:

1. From the start, with no change to Puddle: a Wellyboot BI data source is a Puddle export. The author exports Parquet (preferred: typed, compact, range-readable) or CSV/JSON/NDJSON from an Output node and drops it into Wellyboot BI. Wellyboot BI reads it with the same DuckDB readers Puddle uses.
2. Later, with changes in the Puddle repository (listed below as dependencies): Puddle stamps its Parquet exports with provenance in the file's key-value metadata, and gains a "Publish to Wellyboot BI" delivery that posts an Output node's rows to a Wellyboot BI server the author has signed in to. Both stay opt-in so Puddle's promise holds: data leaves the browser only when the author sends it somewhere.

Puddle-side dependencies (to be raised as issues in `kevinmcaleer/puddle`):

- P1. Provenance in Parquet exports: `compileExport` in `src/compiler/export.ts` adds `KV_METADATA` to the Parquet `COPY` options with the project name, Output node name, export time, source head hashes and the names of rules that passed. Wellyboot BI reads it with DuckDB's `parquet_kv_metadata()`. Without it, Wellyboot BI shows the file name and schema only. Needed for the provenance panel in Phase 2; optional otherwise.
- P2. A "Publish to Wellyboot BI" delivery: a new `Delivery` in `src/export/` that posts the export to a Wellyboot BI server, with the Wellyboot BI author credential kept in IndexedDB the way the sync layer keeps its credentials (`CredentialStore` and `idbCredentials` in `src/sync/providers.ts`). Needed for the one-click flow in Phase 10; until then the export-and-drop flow works.
- P3. Nothing is needed for reading Wellyboot BI datasets back into Puddle beyond Wellyboot BI sending CORS headers; that is on the Wellyboot BI side (Phase 6).

## Security model for public share links

A share link makes a dashboard, and the data it needs, readable by anyone who has the link. The model is designed around that fact rather than pretending otherwise.

- Explicit publish. Nothing is reachable from a server until the author publishes. Publishing uploads the exact datasets the dashboard uses and a frozen copy of the dashboard. Local-only dashboards never leave the browser.
- Unguessable links. A share link is `https://<wellyboot>/s/<id>` where the id is at least 128 bits from a cryptographically secure random source, encoded base64url. Ids are stored hashed, so a leaked database does not leak working links.
- Scoped tokens. Opening a share link gives the browser a short-lived, read-only access token scoped to that one published dashboard and the dataset versions it references. The token cannot list, read or query anything else, and cannot see the author's other dashboards or datasets. Embed tokens are scoped tighter still: to one visual and its one dataset.
- Read-only. The public API offers only: fetch the published dashboard document, fetch the referenced dataset files (range requests allowed), and fetch a pre-rendered snapshot. There is no public write, and the server runs no SQL from the public.
- Whole-dataset exposure is stated plainly. Because queries run in the viewer's browser against the dataset file, a link holder can read every row and column of the datasets the dashboard uses, not just the aggregates shown. The publish dialog says this before the first publish. Authors who need to hide columns or rows remove them in Puddle before exporting.
- Revocable. Every share link and embed token can be turned off from the author's Published panel; the server refuses it within one request, and dataset files are no longer served under it. Dataset versions no longer referenced by any live link are deleted.
- Rate-limited and metered. Per link and per client address: requests per minute and bytes per hour, with sensible defaults in the server's settings and a clear "This dashboard is busy, try again shortly" message in the viewer. Usage counts (opens, bytes) are shown to the author.
- Author authentication. Publishing requires signing in to the Wellyboot BI server as an author. The first release supports a server-configured author key (self-hosted, one or a few authors); GitHub sign-in is an open question.
- Hygiene. Share pages send `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` so the link id is not leaked to third-party sites in embedded content, `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` by default (the author can opt a dashboard in to indexing), and a strict Content-Security-Policy. Dataset files are served with `Content-Disposition: attachment` only from the download endpoint, not the range endpoint, and with CORS limited to the Wellyboot BI origins unless the author turns on "Readable by Puddle".

## Stack

Matched to Puddle so the two share a design system, conventions and tests, unless noted:

- Node 22, npm workspaces, TypeScript 5.9, ESLint 9 flat config (Puddle's `eslint.config.js`), Prettier-free style as in Puddle.
- Web: Vite 7, React 19, Tailwind 3 with Puddle's `tailwind.preset.js`, Zustand 5, Zod 4, lucide-react, `@duckdb/duckdb-wasm` and `apache-arrow`, the Puddle design system vendored into `src/design-system/` and `src/ui/`.
- Charts: Vega-Lite (`vega`, `vega-lite`, `vega-embed`). Chosen because it is declarative JSON like the rest of the model, renders to canvas or SVG, exports a self-contained HTML embed through `vega-embed`, covers every chart type in this epic including maps, and has accessible tooltips and aria descriptions. Our chart spec compiles to Vega-Lite the way Puddle's steps compile to SQL, so the rendering library can be swapped later. (Not Glide Data Grid or React Flow, which Puddle uses for its grid and node canvas; the table visual uses Glide Data Grid, and the canvas is a layout grid.)
- Server: Node 22, Hono (small, standards-based, TypeScript-first), SQLite through `better-sqlite3`, dataset files on a volume. Optional later: `@duckdb/node-api` for server-side snapshots and queries.
- Tests: Vitest 3 (shared and isolated projects as in Puddle's `vite.config.ts`), engine tests on the Node build of DuckDB-WASM, Playwright 1.56 with `@axe-core/playwright`, `fake-indexeddb`, `fast-check`.
- Deployment: Docker Compose with an nginx image for the web app and a Node image for the server, multi-arch (amd64 and arm64), behind a Cloudflare Tunnel; a GitHub Actions CI that runs lint, typecheck, unit, engine and Playwright tests and builds the images, after Puddle's `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.
- Docs: a Sphinx user guide in `docs/` with Playwright-taken screenshots, as Puddle does.
- Licence: MIT, as Puddle.

## Phases

Each phase is a sub-issue, sized to be built and reviewed as a chunk, in this order.

- [ ] #1 Phase 1: Project scaffold, design system and CI
- [ ] #2 Phase 2: Puddle datasets and the data source picker
- [ ] #3 Phase 3: Query model and SQL compiler
- [ ] #4 Phase 4: Visual editor with bar, line and pie charts
- [ ] #5 Phase 5: Dashboards, canvas layout, save and load, slicers
- [ ] #6 Phase 6: Wellyboot BI server and publishing
- [ ] #7 Phase 7: Share links with scoped public access
- [ ] #8 Phase 8: Publish a single chart to embeddable HTML
- [ ] #9 Phase 9: More chart types
- [ ] #10 Phase 10: Polish, hardening, docs, deployment and the Puddle round trip

## Open questions

1. Report versus dashboard. Power BI separates reports (pages of visuals) from dashboards (pinned tiles). Should Wellyboot BI add pages to a dashboard later, or keep one canvas per dashboard and let authors link dashboards? Default for this epic: one canvas, with "pages" noted as a possible follow-on.
2. Server-side query. Serving Parquet to the browser is simple and keeps the server free of SQL from the public, but a dashboard over a 2 GB dataset will not work on a phone. Should Phase 7 or a later phase add a server-side query mode (DuckDB in Node, running only compiled queries from published dashboards, never free SQL) for large datasets, which would also allow hiding columns from link holders?
3. Author sign-in. A server-configured author key is enough for a single self-hoster. Is GitHub OAuth (the server can now hold the client secret, which Puddle's browser-only Gist sync could not) wanted for a shared instance?
4. Chart library. Vega-Lite is proposed. ECharts is the alternative (larger chart menu, faster canvas rendering for very large series, weaker standalone embed story). Decide before Phase 4 starts.
5. Dataset size limits in the browser. Puddle stores file handles rather than file bytes because sources can exceed memory. Wellyboot BI proposes storing dataset bytes in the origin private file system with a per-dataset cap (say 500 MB) and falling back to a file handle above it. Is a cap acceptable?
6. Live embeds and third-party cookies. A live embed in someone else's site loads data from Wellyboot BI with an embed token in the URL, with no cookies. Is a referrer allow-list per embed (so the token only works when the embedding page is on a named site) wanted in the first release, or later?
7. Should Wellyboot BI read `.puddle.json` project files at all? It could show the lineage (which steps produced the dataset) next to a data source if the author drops the project file in too. Nice to have, not planned.
8. Where should "Publish to Wellyboot BI" live in Puddle: as a new Output format next to CSV and Parquet, or as a delivery choice on the existing Parquet export? The latter keeps `OutputSpecZ` unchanged.

items.title: Complete Dashboard API v1 parity and migrate dashboard to shared JSON contract for WebOS/Android
items.body:
## Goal
Complete the existing `/api/v1` as the canonical read-only representation of everything available in the Reports dashboard, then make the HTML/htmx dashboard consume the same shared application/service contract. Future WebOS/Android clients are **out of scope**.

## Existing baseline (avoid duplication)
- `src/ocpp_reports/api_v1.py` already exposes `/api/v1/summary`, `/connectors`, `/transactions`, `/stations`, `/filters`, `/openapi.json`, registered by `web.py`.
- `web.py` also exposes legacy `/api/snapshot`, `/api/event-group`, and HTML transaction detail. These are existing routes; prior Reports HTTP contracts are not a compatibility requirement after coordinated fleet upgrade.
- Current v1 has incomplete parity: transactions only support view/page with hardcoded empty term/status/location/date and UTC; no JSON transaction detail, event group/history, source synchronization/freshness, timezone options, or complete dashboard filter/view semantics. Current dashboard still assembles HTML data via `read` rather than consuming the v1 contract.
- Preserve existing login/auth middleware, source allowlists, admin/operator/customer separation, tenant isolation and no-write behavior. Coordinate with #111, #114, #162, #185/#188 rather than duplicating their fixes.

## Acceptance criteria
1. Inventory all dashboard panels and fields (status summary, connectors/station 0/individual, source/station/location filters, transaction list/details, event groups, active energy, power, SoC, synchronization and provenance/freshness, timestamps and selectable timezones). Record field-to-endpoint parity matrix and unknown/unavailable semantics.
2. Versioned JSON schemas with stable pagination, validation, timestamps, timezone behavior, explicit nulls, error handling, OpenAPI examples; reuse existing warehouse projections and business rules (no second business logic).
3. Tenant and role-scoped authorization on **every** endpoint, including ID enumeration, details, filters, pagination, event history; reject cross-tenant requests, no information leakage, no unsafe CORS or unauthenticated fallback.
4. Dashboard and API use one application service/query layer; migrate dashboard without breaking HTML, htmx refresh/scroll, login/profile/password, current supported URLs. Preserve p95 <1s benchmark target.
5. Automated parity tests (HTML vs JSON for identical filters), negative auth/tenant tests, rebuild-from-forwarders verification (cursor-zero replay, counts, transaction/event evidence) and empty data tests, timezone/DST, energy/status aggregation and pagination, OpenAPI contract tests.
6. CI green, review and merge incremental PRs; deploy through the existing idempotent Ansible pipeline once, verify live API/dashboard and document acceptance. Follow the repository FIX-FORWARD policy: correct defects with a subsequent tested commit/deployment; preserve historical source SQLite evidence and rebuild Collector from retained Forwarder journals; old Reports binaries, prior HTTP contracts and unsupported export schemas need not remain compatible. Rollback, version reversal and Ansible compensations are not acceptance criteria. No WebOS/Android UI implementation.

## Upgrade scope
All Reports installations will be upgraded to the new version. No backwards compatibility requirement for old Reports releases or retired HTTP endpoints. Verify the supported current producer export schema separately; do not retain `ocpp-csms/export/v1` solely for compatibility unless it remains a supported input. Preserve Forwarder source SQLite evidence. Rebuild the Collector from a new empty database by replaying its complete retained local replication journals, verifying per-source cursors, counts and evidence. Collector schema migration is not mandatory when rebuild succeeds; do not delete old Collector before acceptance. This is a coordinated FIX-FORWARD upgrade.

## Suggested increments
A. Extract shared dashboard query/projection layer + parity inventory; B. complete v1 endpoints/filters/detail and schemas; C. migrate HTML/htmx to shared contract; D. auth/performance regression, deploy and field validation.

Do not close until deployed API and dashboard are verified against the same data and source-scoped identities.

## Collector rebuild acceptance (preproduction, November 2026)
- Audit retention/purge paths and confirm each Forwarder local `replication_changes` journal can be replayed from sequence zero. Absence of manual purges alone is not sufficient proof.
- Validate isolated new Collector ingest with paginated journal replay, matching source-specific event/transaction/rating/connector evidence, last sequence, and idempotent retries.
- **Current forwarder state is monotonic:** `forward_cursors` persists acknowledgments and `save_cursor` refuses regressions. A new Collector at cursor zero cannot be repopulated by an unchanged running Forwarder with an advanced cursor. Design and test an explicitly authorized, bounded replay/reseed mechanism before any real cutover; do not mutate production cursors during CI.
- Retain old Collector and all Forwarder databases until reconstruction has passed and been explicitly approved. No automatic rollback or Ansible compensation.
- A partial retained history must be reported as partial, not silently labeled complete. No compatibility requirement for old Reports releases or retired HTTP contracts.
